title: TRR tracker overflow fixed with per-row analog hammer integrators
idea: Target Row Refresh died to TRRespass/Blacksmith because its few-entry aggressor table overflowed under many-sided patterns. Fix exactly that: each wordline driver gets a tiny leaky MIM capacitor that receives a fixed charge packet per ACT, a shared comparator fires a neighbor refresh when it crosses threshold, and the leak rate matches the refresh window, so there is no table to overflow or game.
why: Row hammer at ~1k ACT (fact 9): deterministic, pattern-independent protection for ~1-2% array area versus digital per-row counters and their tRC penalty; lets denser, more hammer-prone cells ship.

title: PARA revived with sacrificial hammer-canary cells between rows
idea: PARA (probabilistic adjacent-row activation) was never adopted because at ~1k-ACT thresholds its trigger probability must be so high that blind neighbor refreshes eat bandwidth. Fix: place a strip of deliberately hammer-sensitive canary cells (thinner isolation, smaller Cs) along each wordline pair, read through a cheap dedicated sense line, and refresh neighbors only when a canary has physically flipped.
why: Mitigation triggered by physical evidence instead of dice rolls: ~5-10x fewer mitigation refreshes than PARA at equal safety, recovering ~3-8% bandwidth at 1k-ACT thresholds (fact 9).

title: RAIDR's VRT killer exposed by accelerated trap-toggle burn-in screening
idea: Multi-rate refresh (RAIDR) died because Variable Retention Time cells jump between strong and weak bins after profiling. Fix exactly that at test: a burn-in recipe alternating high temperature, negative-wordline and GIDL-stress phases forces trap occupancy to toggle hundreds of times in minutes, so VRT-prone cells reveal themselves and are fused to spare rows before binning.
why: Makes retention-binned refresh safe: 2-4x longer refresh interval for >99.9% of rows, cutting the ~46 fJ/bit refresh tax and 10-20% bandwidth loss (fact 3).

title: Flikker's annotation burden removed by hardware bit-plane splitting of tensors
idea: Flikker-style approximate refresh failed because programmers had to hand-mark non-critical data. Fix: the memory controller transposes words on pages whose dtype (bf16/fp8/int8) is known from the ML allocator, so sign/exponent bits land in fully refreshed rows while low mantissa bits land in rows refreshed 16x less often that tolerate ~1e-4 BER.
why: ~50-60% of AI tensor bits move to relaxed rows: ~45% refresh energy cut (fact 3) and rows of weaker cells become sellable, with negligible accuracy loss.

title: DDR5 on-die ECC miscorrection fixed by exposing syndromes to host
idea: DDR5's on-die SEC hides raw errors and can miscorrect a double error into a triple error that host Chipkill then misses. Fix: return the on-die syndrome bits in spare burst slots or a metadata sideband so the host decodes a true concatenated product code that knows which symbols the die already touched.
why: Restores end-to-end ECC strength so vendors can ship ~10x higher raw-BER cells (smaller Cs, relaxed tail screening, fact 1) at the same system FIT.

title: Abolish consumer non-ECC segmentation; create a cheaper raw-BER-graded die bin
idea: Decades of withholding ECC from consumer platforms forced every DIMM to be near-zero-defect, so dies with a handful of weak cells are scrapped or dumped. Fix via U.S. federal procurement rules plus a JEDEC grade: ECC mandatory on all new platforms, and a formal 'raw BER <=1e-6' die bin sold at a discount into ECC-only channels.
why: Recovers an estimated 5-10% of dies/rows lost at test as sellable bits without a new fab; raises supply and cuts cost per usable bit.

title: Optane wear tail decoded as erasures to double Reed-Solomon power
idea: 3D XPoint carried heavy ECC and indirection latency to cover its wear-out tail. Fix: per-line write counters in out-of-band metadata plus a per-cell wear model flag near-dead bits, which are passed to the Reed-Solomon decoder as erasures, since an erasure costs one parity symbol instead of two.
why: Same parity covers ~2x more worn bits, giving 3-5x longer life or half the ECC overhead for any wear-limited DRAM substitute (cost per bit, endurance).

title: Z-RAM retention tail cancelled by differential twin floating bodies
idea: Innovative Silicon's Z-RAM died when floating-body retention and disturb variability blew up at 45 nm and AMD walked away. Fix: store each bit as complementary hole charge in two adjacent floating bodies sharing a well and sense them differentially, so common-mode junction leakage and temperature-driven loss cancel and only mismatch decays.
why: Capacitor-free cell (attacks the charge wall, fact 1) with ~10x tighter retention tail at 2 transistors per bit, still smaller and simpler than 1T1C with a 70:1 pillar.

title: T-RAM temperature failure fixed by replica-thyristor closed-loop gate biasing
idea: T-RAM stalled at GlobalFoundries because thyristor holding current swings by orders of magnitude from 0 to 105 C, losing data hot and writing slowly cold. Fix: every mat carries a replica thyristor whose holding current an on-die loop servos by adjusting the shared gate-assist voltage, keeping all cells a fixed margin above holding across temperature and aging.
why: Makes a capacitor-less one-device cell robust across corners, removing the capacitor wall and much sensing periphery (facts 1, 7).

title: HP memristor variability averaged by five-device vertical voting pillars
idea: HP's TaOx memristor program died on device-to-device variability and random forming. Fix: build five tiny switching layers in parallel along one vertical pillar so the sense amp reads their summed conductance; variability shrinks by ~sqrt(5) and one dead device costs margin, not data.
why: Tolerates ~30%-sigma devices without verify loops; in 3D the extra tiers are cheap, so density barely drops while yield rises sharply.

title: Racetrack shift errors fixed with disk-style servo markers and self-clocking codes
idea: IBM's racetrack memory stalled because domain walls pin or overshoot, so one bad shift offsets every following bit. Fix: borrow hard-disk servo practice by interleaving fixed marker domains and writing data in a run-length-limited self-clocking code, so the read head detects any over- or under-shift and re-shifts before decoding.
why: Turns catastrophic positional errors into ordinary correctable symbols, enabling capacitor-free magnetic shift memory with many bits per access device (density, fact 1).

title: FeRAM imprint cancelled by scheduled whole-row polarity inversion
idea: Ferroelectric RAM (PZT, now HZO) fails by imprint: cells left in one state shift their coercive voltage until they will not switch or sense. Fix: a per-row inversion flag, so whenever a row is written its data is stored inverted with the flag toggled and every capacitor spends about half its life in each polarization, cancelling imprint.
why: Widens sense margin at high temperature, allowing thinner, lower-voltage HZO (voltage floor, fact 10) and longer retention.

title: MLC PCM resistance drift neutralized by co-written in-line reference cells
idea: Multi-level phase-change memory was abandoned largely because amorphous resistance drifts as t^0.1, collapsing level margins. Fix: each line writes three reference cells at the intermediate levels in the same pulse train, and reads compare data cells against those references, which drift identically, so thresholds track automatically.
why: Restores 2 bits/cell PCM (2x density) without periodic reprogramming.

title: STT-MRAM asymmetric write errors absorbed by Z-channel codes
idea: STT-MRAM lost the DRAM-replacement race partly because write error rate demands high current, and failures are strongly one-directional (P to AP). Fix: deliberately lower write current until errors are almost purely in that direction, then protect with asymmetric Z-channel codes (Varshamov/Constantin-Rao style) that correct only that direction.
why: ~30% lower write current/energy or ~40% less parity at equal uncorrectable rate; a smaller access transistor raises density.

title: Samsung's withdrawn PRAM fixed by checkerboard thermal-phase write scheduling
idea: Samsung's mobile PRAM never scaled partly because RESET heat partially crystallizes neighboring cells (thermal disturb). Fix: the write scheduler splits each array into four checkerboard phases and never writes adjacent cells within one thermal time constant (~100 ns), so each phase's idle neighbors act as heat sinks.
why: Permits ~30% tighter pitch (density) without disturb-induced retention loss.

title: Crossbar sneak paths decoded as signal via multi-bias network inversion
idea: Selector-less resistive crossbars (HP, Crossbar Inc.) died because sneak currents corrupt reads in large arrays. Fix: read each small tile under K pseudo-random bias patterns and solve the resistor-network inverse problem (belief propagation / least squares) for every cell conductance, treating sneak current as known mixing rather than noise.
why: Enables true 4F2 selector-free arrays with no selector material or mask, trading extra read energy for ~1.5x density and fewer process steps.

title: IBM MXT compression repurposed only to make room for in-line ECC
idea: IBM's MXT memory compression (Pinnacle, 2001) died of latency and allocation complexity. Fix exactly that by compressing only enough to free 8-16 bytes per 64-byte line (fixed size, no reallocation) and storing a strong symbol code in the freed space, with incompressible lines falling back to a small parity region.
why: Chipkill-class protection on non-ECC x8/x16 DIMMs and LPDDR, so cheaper higher-BER parts can serve servers; ~12% capacity saved versus ECC DIMMs.

title: Williams-tube read-around ratio revived as per-die fused hammer threshold
idea: Williams-tube memories lost to core, but had a working discipline: each tube's measured 'read-around ratio' set how many neighboring reads were allowed before regeneration. Fix today's worst-case row-hammer design the same way: test each die's real hammer threshold per bank, fuse it into a mode register, scale controller mitigation per bank, and price dies by threshold grade.
why: Stops sizing every die's mitigation for the worst die (~1k ACT, fact 9): typical dies run 3-10x less mitigation, and low-threshold dies are sold rather than scrapped.

title: ArchShield fault maps replaced by in-row stuck-aware scrambler masks
idea: ArchShield-style weak-cell fault maps died on lookup latency and OS-reserved memory. Fix: leaky cells only lose the charged state, so treat them as 'partially stuck at 0' (Kuznetsov-Tsybakov defect coding); each row stores its weak-cell positions in a few spare cells that are read for free when the row opens, and on-die logic picks one of 4-8 scrambler masks that leaves those cells discharged, saving the mask ID with the line.
why: Retention-weak cells stop causing errors at ~0.5% overhead, so smaller-Cs or leakier cells become acceptable (charge wall fact 1, leakage tail fact 3).

title: Error-correcting pointers rescued from PCM to absorb DRAM hard faults
idea: Error-Correcting Pointers (ECP) were invented for PCM wear-out and died with it. Fix by moving them to DRAM: each 64B line gets 2-3 pointer-plus-replacement-bit entries in on-die spare cells, populated in the field when scrubbing finds a permanently failing bit, so SECDED stays reserved for soft errors.
why: Absorbs the growing hard-fault tail of shrinking capacitors and TSV-stressed HBM dies (fact 6), raising usable yield ~5-10% and extending field life.

title: Macronix self-healing heater idea reborn as wordline Joule annealing
idea: Macronix's 2012 self-healing flash (on-chip heaters annealing oxide traps) never shipped because dedicated heaters cost area and power. Fix: use the existing buried wordline itself as the heater, so rows that ECC or scrubbing flag for rising leakage get millisecond high-current pulses that anneal the access-transistor interface traps driving the leakage tail.
why: In-field self-healing of retention and hammer-induced trap damage; shrinks the <=13 fA leakage tail (fact 3) over life instead of letting it grow, enabling longer refresh intervals.

title: IBM RAIM moved inside the bank: parity rows rebuild hammered victims
idea: IBM's RAIM (RAID across memory channels) protects against whole-DIMM loss but never addressed row-level bursts such as hammer victims, which exceed per-line ECC. Fix: on-die logic maintains one XOR parity row per group of 32 rows in a subarray, updated on writes, so any single row corrupted beyond ECC is rebuilt from its siblings.
why: Converts row-hammer and single-row retention bursts into recoverable events, letting mitigation thresholds relax ~2-4x (fact 9) at ~3% capacity cost.

title: Spectek-style weak-die salvage into ECC-heavy CXL inference modules
idea: Off-spec DRAM is sold through salvage channels into toys and low-end goods because nothing makes weak dies server-grade. Fix: a startup buys sub-spec dies (retention or hammer fails) and builds CXL modules whose controller runs per-die refresh rates, LDPC across dies and a hot-spare die, sold as KV-cache and inference capacity.
why: Turns ~3-8% of output now sold near scrap into data-center bits at ~40% lower $/GB, adding supply with zero fab capex.

title: Z-RAM refresh eliminated by buried-well BJT feedback bistable bodies
idea: Z-RAM failed partly because floating-body charge leaked out in milliseconds and needed refresh. Fix: add a buried n-well beneath each floating body so the parasitic vertical BJT continuously replenishes holes by impact ionization when the body is charged and stays off when empty (Zeno-style bistable floating body), latching both states statically.
why: Zero refresh power: the latch self-restores, so disturb- or alpha-induced charge loss heals automatically; a capacitor-free 1T cell attacks facts 1, 3 and 9, provided holding current stays in the pA range.

title: Bubble memory's bias-magnet killer removed with zero-field skyrmion loops
idea: Magnetic bubble memory (TI, Intel Magnetics) never needed refresh but died because it required permanent bias magnets and coil drives, making it slow and bulky. Fix: use exchange-biased synthetic-antiferromagnet multilayers that stabilize skyrmions at zero applied field, move them with spin-orbit current around loops, and keep bubble memory's proven major/minor-loop redundancy with an on-chip bad-loop map.
why: Nonvolatile with zero refresh, built-in yield repair from loop sparing, and many bits per access transistor for density without a capacitor.

title: FeRAM read fatigue removed by sub-coercive nondestructive capacitance readout
idea: Ramtron-era FeRAM's destructive read made every read a write, fatiguing cells and costing restore energy. Fix: read with a small sub-coercive AC probe that senses the polarization-dependent asymmetry of the capacitor's C-V curve (piezo/dielectric nonlinearity), leaving the domain state untouched.
why: Nonvolatile and refresh-free; reads consume no endurance, so ~1e10-cycle HZO acts as effectively unlimited endurance for read-heavy data, and no restore cycle is needed (fact 8).

title: eDRAM's refresh burden replaced by decay-as-miss caches
idea: Intel's Crystal Well and IBM POWER eDRAM caches were dropped partly over refresh power and hot retention. Fix: never refresh; each line carries a coarse write-epoch tag, any line older than its retention budget or failing ECC is treated as a cache miss and refetched, and dirty lines are evicted before their epoch expires.
why: Zero refresh power; the retention tail becomes a slight miss-rate increase, so dense eDRAM or stacked-DRAM cache dies can use leaky, cheap cells (fact 3).

title: EnerJ approximate storage fixed with age-aware asymmetric soft decoding
idea: EnerJ-style approximate storage never caught on because developers had to annotate types and accept silent errors. Fix: no refresh at all for buffers with a declared lifetime (activations, gradients, KV blocks); each write is time-stamped, and the decoder feeds elapsed age and the known 1-to-0 leakage direction as soft priors into an LDPC decode, recovering data exactly until the age limit.
why: Zero refresh power with exact, not approximate, results for data living under ~1 s, saving 16-33% of idle power (fact 3) and admitting weaker cells.

title: Smart Refresh counters replaced by streaming sweep-coverage proofs
idea: Smart Refresh (skipping refresh for recently accessed rows) died because per-row timestamp counters cost area and gave no coverage guarantee. Fix: accelerators that stream every weight row each iteration order reads as a strict per-bank address sweep, so one sweep pointer plus a deadline timer proves every row was activated within tREFW; the refresh engine is disabled, and if the workload stalls past the deadline the region is marked stale and reloaded from its persistent copy.
why: Zero refresh power and zero refresh bandwidth loss (10-20%, fact 3) for weight-resident HBM.

title: Cryogenic DRAM revived where cooling already exists: 77 K no-refresh tier
idea: Cryogenic memory efforts (IBM's Josephson program, later cryo-DRAM studies) died on the cost of dedicated cooling. Fix: place a DRAM tier inside LN2 loops already present in immersion-cooled AI pods or HTS power distribution, where junction and subthreshold leakage collapse and retention stretches far beyond typical data lifetimes; refresh is disabled and data older than the qualified retention is poisoned and restored by software.
why: Zero refresh power plus lower wire resistance; the leakage tail (fact 3) effectively vanishes, allowing smaller capacitors (fact 1).

title: Cavendish NEMS memory's stiction killer turned into the latching mechanism
idea: Cavendish Kinetics' NEMS memory pivoted away because cantilevers stuck unpredictably (stiction). Fix: design for controlled stiction, using a self-assembled monolayer that sets adhesion energy inside a narrow window so a beam latched to the 'on' contact stays put unpowered, while a counter-electrode pulse plus the beam's spring force releases it reliably.
why: Mechanically bistable: zero refresh, no leakage tail, immune to radiation and row hammer, BEOL-buildable over CMOS with no capacitor.

title: TI tunneling SRAM fixed with self-trimmed silicon interband tunnel diodes
idea: TI's tunneling SRAM (a resonant-tunneling diode pair latching a DRAM storage node) died because III-V peak currents varied too much across wafers. Fix: use low-temperature Si/SiGe interband tunnel diodes grown in BEOL, plus a per-mat replica diode and electrical trim pulse that sets the valley-current bias, so each node sits in one of two stable points with pA standby.
why: Static, zero-refresh cell near DRAM density, with the tunnel-diode latch restoring any leakage or hammer-induced charge loss (facts 3, 9).

title: FeFET retention loss cured by capacitance-matched floating-metal MFMIS stacks
idea: 1T FeFET memory stalled because the depolarization field and interface charge trapping erase stored polarization in hours to days at temperature. Fix: insert a floating metal gate and size the ferroelectric area at 1/4-1/10 of the MOS area (MFMIS) so the ferroelectric sees almost no depolarizing field, and replace the SiO2 interlayer with a thin high-k layer to cut trapping.
why: Nonvolatile, zero-refresh 1T cell with no capacitor (fact 1); the retention tail is removed by electrostatic design rather than refresh.

title: Optane endurance shielded by MMU write-budget traps and page migration
idea: 3D XPoint never displaced DRAM partly because ~1e7-1e8-cycle media wore out under hot writes. Fix: the MMU keeps a per-page write-budget counter, and a page exceeding its budget traps and migrates to a small SRAM-backed write log, so only read-mostly data (weights, code, indexes) ever lives in the nonvolatile tier.
why: Zero refresh for the bulk tier (read-mostly data is often >70% of AI-server bytes) with a guaranteed 5-year wear life; cuts DRAM bits needed.

title: Antiferromagnetic memory's weak readout fixed with Mn3Sn tunnel junctions
idea: CuMnAs electrically switched antiferromagnetic memory stalled because its readout signal (anisotropic magnetoresistance ~0.1%) was too weak. Fix: use noncollinear antiferromagnets such as Mn3Sn or Mn3Pt, whose momentum-space spin splitting yields large tunneling magnetoresistance in an all-antiferromagnet tunnel junction, while keeping spin-orbit-torque switching.
why: Nonvolatile and zero refresh, with no stray fields, so neighbor disturb (a row-hammer analogue) and external-field upsets vanish; picosecond-scale dynamics.

title: Cray's SRAM main memory revived at near-threshold with ECC-mapped Vmin failures
idea: Cray-1 and other supercomputers used SRAM main memory until DRAM's cost won. Fix the cost and power that killed it: CFET-stacked 6T SRAM in monolithic 3D tiers run at ~0.45 V, where leakage collapses but ~1e-4 cells fail, with a test-time row-sparing map plus SECDED absorbing the low-Vmin failures.
why: Static storage: zero refresh, no capacitor, buildable in U.S. logic fabs; ECC turns low-voltage unreliability into a ~4x leakage cut.

title: HP/UCLA molecular crossbar's yield killer solved by defect-mapped stochastic decoders
idea: The 2007 160-kbit rotaxane molecular memory worked, but only ~25% of bits were usable and its decoders could not be lithographed at that pitch. Fix: adopt Teramac-style defect tolerance with nanowire decoders formed stochastically (random doping codes) and mapped at power-up, writing data only to verified bistable junctions through a logical-to-physical map with rateless coding across junctions.
why: Bistable molecular switches need no refresh; even accepting 75% defects at a few nm2 per bit could beat DRAM density by 10x or more.

title: Crossbar Inc. ReRAM stuck faults self-healed by ECC-triggered reforming
idea: Crossbar Inc. and other ReRAM ventures lost DRAM-class ambitions to stuck-at-set/reset cells that accumulate with cycling. Fix: when the decoder corrects the same bit twice, the controller fires a reverse-polarity 'reforming' pulse that dissolves the overgrown or ruptured filament and re-forms it, returning the cell to service instead of retiring it.
why: Nonvolatile and zero refresh; in-field self-healing extends usable endurance ~10x and tolerates cheaper, less uniform films.

title: FeRAM's fab-poisoning PZT replaced by built-in-biased antiferroelectric ZrO2 capacitors
idea: Ramtron FeRAM never entered DRAM fabs because lead-based PZT contaminated lines and did not scale. Fix: use the ZrO2 that DRAM capacitors already deposit, an antiferroelectric, between asymmetric work-function electrodes (e.g., TiN bottom, high-work-function RuO2 top) whose built-in field shifts one double-hysteresis loop to zero bias, making the capacitor bistable and nonvolatile.
why: Zero refresh using existing DRAM dielectric and tools; antiferroelectric switching endures far more cycles than ferroelectric HZO, approaching DRAM-class endurance.

title: Optane distrust fixed by endurance-as-a-service telemetry warranties
idea: Part of what killed Optane was buyers' fear of wear-out and an opaque, single-vendor reliability story. Fix: sell nonvolatile CXL memory by the write, not the module, with devices streaming per-region wear and corrected-error telemetry, a per-petabyte-written warranty, and pre-emptive module swaps before the uncorrectable rate crosses a contract threshold.
why: De-risks refresh-free nonvolatile tiers for hyperscalers, removing refresh power from the bulk of capacity and moving reliability risk to the party with the data.

title: IBM Josephson memory density fixed with NbN kinetic-inductance persistent loops
idea: IBM's 1980s Josephson computer was cancelled largely because superconducting loop memory cells were microns wide and Pb-alloy junctions failed on thermal cycling. Fix: store bits as persistent supercurrent in ~100 nm NbN nanowire loops whose kinetic inductance replaces bulky geometric inductance, with cycling-robust Nb/AlOx junctions and moats that trap stray flux away from cells.
why: Persistent currents need zero refresh and dissipate nothing while holding; dense cryogenic main memory for superconducting or cryo-CMOS AI accelerators.

title: Nantero NRAM's random-fabric variability replaced by crossed aligned nanotube bilayers
idea: Nantero's NRAM spent two decades unshipped at scale partly because spin-coated random CNT fabric gave cell-to-cell differences in junction count and switching. Fix: deposit two layers of pre-aligned, sorted nanotubes crossed at 90 degrees (Langmuir-Schaefer or floating evaporative assembly) so every cell contains the same number of tube-tube junctions.
why: Van-der-Waals-latched, zero-refresh cell with a tight distribution, removing verify loops and spare overhead; BEOL-compatible and radiation hard.

title: Adesto CBRAM filament randomness pinned by single-nanopore 2D interlayers
idea: CBRAM (Adesto and others) stayed out of dense memory because metal filaments form at random sites, giving wide resistance spread and high-temperature retention loss. Fix: insert a monolayer hBN barrier with exactly one electron-beam or ion-milled nanopore per cell, so the filament always nucleates in the same ~2 nm spot and its neck is mechanically constrained.
why: Deterministic, zero-refresh resistive cell with tight distributions and better retention, enabling smaller margins and multi-level storage.

title: LPDDR PASR's failure fixed by expiring, poisonable no-refresh memory zones
idea: LPDDR's partial-array self-refresh was rarely used because operating systems could not guarantee which data was disposable. Fix: OS 'ephemeral zones' are never refreshed; allocations there carry a deadline (KV-cache blocks, activations, network buffers), the memory controller poisons any line past its deadline, and the runtime recomputes it (e.g., re-prefill the KV block) on a poisoned read.
why: Zero refresh power for an estimated 30-60% of AI-server memory, with correctness guaranteed by poison semantics instead of stored charge.

title: Flash-as-DRAM endurance killer fixed by triple-barrier resonant-tunneling storage
idea: Attempts to use floating-gate flash as working memory died on tunnel-oxide wear (~1e5 cycles) and high write voltage. Fix: replace the oxide with an InAs/AlSb triple-barrier resonant-tunneling structure that is opaque at rest but passes electrons at a ~2.5 V resonance, so charge enters the floating gate without hot-carrier damage (UltraRAM-style).
why: Nonvolatile, zero refresh, low-voltage writes with reported >1e7 cycles; a capacitor-free 1T cell with a path toward DRAM-class endurance.

title: Federal commons for dead refresh-free memory IP plus shared qualification line
idea: Most refresh-free memory ventures (T-RAM, Z-RAM, Kilopass, Spin Memory and others) died less from physics than from missing reliability data and qualified second sources. Fix: a federal program buys or licenses their patent estates into an open pool and funds a shared U.S. qualification line that runs JEDEC-style retention, endurance, disturb and soft-error testing on every revived cell and publishes the failure-rate data.
why: Cuts years and tens of $M from each zero-refresh technology's path to qualification, lowering capital intensity and lifting U.S. manufacturability.
